Search is hybrid by default: ids in the query come first, then a dense and a lexical leg are fused (the lexical weight is semantic.lexical_weight, 0.3). Add --reranker llm (any OpenAI-compatible chat model, KEEL_RERANK_BASE_URL / _MODEL / _API_KEY) or --reranker http (the Cohere, Jina or Voyage /rerank API) to reorder the best candidates. For asymmetric embedders set KEEL_EMBEDDINGS_QUERY_PREFIX / _DOCUMENT_PREFIX (e5: "query: ", "passage: "). How much each piece buys, measured: docs/design/semantic-evals.md.

Indexing never runs in ingest, so ingest stays deterministic and offline. Only tenant and global knowledge is indexed: task and agent memory and pending proposals are not. The cartridge decides the rest:

semantic:
  kinds: [card, cliente]
  exclude: [comentario]      # comments full of URLs and technical noise stay out
  relations: [de_cliente]    # "de_cliente: cliente:BAT (nombre: ...)" goes into the card's document

docs.title: Consolidate episodic memory
docs.text:
Agents write task and agent memory that expires. A cartridge's consolidate: section declares which of it becomes a durable fact: the source predicate and scopes (task memory by default; agent memory is private and is read only when from.scopes lists it), an optional within: window on world time (valid_from, so a reingested history keeps its dates), how many observations make a pattern, a reducer (mode, latest, count, min, max, avg, distinct or summary) and the predicate and scope to write. It runs as a job, never in ingest:

uv run keel consolidate examples/fleet --tenant acme-logistics --db keel.db
uv run keel expire acme-logistics --db keel.db --consolidate examples/fleet   # consolidate, then drop expired memory
uv run keel expire --all-tenants --db keel.db --consolidate examples/fleet     # every tenant in the store, one after another

Each run prints written and unchanged per consolidation and is idempotent: the same inputs never write twice. The originals stay until their TTL. reduce: summary needs --summarizer: llm (any OpenAI-compatible chat model, from KEEL_SUMMARIZER_BASE_URL, KEEL_SUMMARIZER_MODEL and KEEL_SUMMARIZER_API_KEY), join (the distinct values joined, deterministic) or your own pkg.module:factory. The other reducers are deterministic and need none.

docs.title: Export the audit trail
docs.text:
One tenant, everything Keel knows about it, as JSONL: entities, relations and facts, closed ones included, each with source, evidence, scope, recorded_at and corrected_by. Hand it to the customer, an auditor, or a diff.

uv run keel export acme-logistics --db keel.db --out acme-logistics.jsonl

Each line is one record: {"record": "fact", "subject": "tire:T-9001", "predicate": "depth_mm", "value": 5.2, "valid_from": ..., "valid_to": ..., "source": "tires.measurements", "evidence": "<event id>", ...}. Another tenant's export never contains this one's rows.

docs.title: Erase a tenant
docs.text:
When an end-customer leaves and the law (Colombia's Ley 1581, GDPR's right to erasure) or your privacy notice says their data goes, Keel deletes everything it stores for that tenant: entities, relations, facts of every scope, what agents and people annotated, the ids of the events it applied and, through the index, its semantic documents. Declare the event your SaaS sends when the customer is deleted:

events:
  household.deleted:
    subject: household
    forgets: tenant      # no handler: Keel erases the event's tenant
    payload: { id: string }

It arrives through the same stream, in order. The erasure is one transaction, and a tombstone (the tenant and the time) stays: any later event for that tenant, an old redelivery included, is skipped (skipped in the report) and annotate is refused, so nothing revives it. The ingest report lists what was deleted (forgotten), and keel consume prints it as a JSON line for your audit log. A second erasure deletes nothing and keeps the first time. The semantic documents go on the next keel index --all-tenants (or keel index --tenant <t>).

From the command line, for one tenant:

uv run keel forget household-42 --db keel.db --index chroma://chroma:8000 --yes
# {"tenant": "household-42", "forgotten_at": "...", "entities": 31, "relations": 40, "facts": 212, "annotations": 3, "ingested": 120, "index": true}

Keel erases only what it stores. The external log is yours: delete or expire the tenant's rows in your outbox table, and remember that consumed queue messages are already gone. Global memory is every tenant's and is kept, so never promote a customer's personal data to it. The tombstone holds the tenant id and the time; pick tenant ids that are not personal data on their own.

docs.title: Contributing to Keel
docs.text: Keel is built in the open, part-time. Small, focused pull requests land fastest.

docs.title: Set up
docs.text:
uv sync --extra dev
uv run pytest
uv run keel validate examples/fleet --events examples/fleet/events.jsonl && uv run keel validate examples/crm --events examples/crm/events.jsonl && uv run keel validate examples/finance --events examples/finance/events.jsonl && uv run keel validate examples/clinics --events examples/clinics/events.jsonl

docs.title: What we are looking for
docs.text:
• Cartridges. The best contribution. A new vertical (clinics, logistics, property management, ...) in examples/<name>/ with cartridge.yaml, handlers.py, a sample stream in events.jsonl and a test in test_<name>.py, like the four already there. It must pass keel validate and require zero changes under keel/. If it does need a core change, open an issue first: that is a bug in the core, and we want to fix it generically.
  • Adapters. Sources that yield Events (see keel/adapters/). An adapter never reads a payload.
  • Bug reports with a failing test. The fastest way to get something fixed.

docs.title: Rules the review enforces
docs.text:
CLAUDE.md is the spec and docs/SPEC.md is the normative contract. The short version:

  1. No domain names under keel/: no entity kind, relation, predicate, rule or event type.
  2. Pointers, not copies. Never copy a row or a table into the graph.
  3. Facts close. Handlers never mutate or delete them.
  4. Five tools. New capability goes into the semantics of the existing five.
  5. Deterministic ingest: no network, no LLM, no randomness.
  6. Every core change comes with a test. Every cartridge change comes with events and assertions.

docs.title: Process
docs.text:
• Open an issue before a large change. For a cartridge or a small fix, a pull request is fine.
  • Run uv run ruff check . and uv run pytest before pushing.
  • Commit messages and all user-facing text in English.
  • If examples/fleet/agent_minimal.py output changes, say why in the pull request.

By contributing you agree that your contributions are licensed under the Apache License 2.0.

docs.title: Against a real Postgres
docs.text:
The table adapter's tests run on sqlite3. To run the same test on Postgres, start one and point KEEL_PG_DSN at it:

docker run -d --rm --name keel-pg -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=keel -p 127.0.0.1:5435:5432 postgres:16-alpine
KEEL_PG_DSN=postgresql://postgres:keel@127.0.0.1:5435/postgres uv run --extra postgres pytest -k real_postgres
docker rm -f keel-pg

docs.title: Against MySQL
docs.text:
The store conformance suite runs on MySQL too (CI does it with a service container). Locally:

docker run -d --rm --name keel-mysql -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=keel -e MYSQL_DATABASE=keel -p 127.0.0.1:3307:3306 mysql:8.4
KEEL_MYSQL_URL=mysql://root:keel@127.0.0.1:3307/keel uv run --extra mysql pytest -q tests/test_store.py
docker rm -f keel-mysql

docs.title: Your own store
docs.text:
The core talks to a Store protocol (keel/store/base.py); MemoryStore is the reference and SqliteStore the default durable one. A third store (Postgres, Graphiti, anything) is a separate package, never a core change. Run the conformance suite against it:

KEEL_STORE=your_pkg.module:factory uv run pytest tests/test_store.py

factory is a zero-argument callable or class that returns a fresh, empty store.

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text:
Bump version in pyproject.toml and __version__ in keel/__init__.py, update the roadmap, then:

git tag -a vX.Y.Z -m "keel-context X.Y.Z" && git push origin vX.Y.Z
gh release create vX.Y.Z --title "X.Y.Z" --notes-file notes.md

The tag triggers .github/workflows/release.yml, which runs the tests, builds and publishes keel-context to PyPI through trusted publishing (one-time setup on PyPI: pending publisher for project keel-context, owner angelkurten, repository keel, workflow release.yml, environment pypi).

The SDK runtimes release separately, when they change, each by pushing its tag; the workflow tests the runtime end to end against keel serve before it publishes:

git tag sdk/typescript/vX.Y.Z && git push origin sdk/typescript/vX.Y.Z   # npm (sdk-typescript-release.yml, trusted publishing); bump sdk/typescript/package.json first
git tag sdk/go/vX.Y.Z && git push origin sdk/go/vX.Y.Z                   # the Go module in this repo (sdk-go-release.yml asks the module proxy for it)
git tag sdk/php/vX.Y.Z && git push origin sdk/php/vX.Y.Z                 # Composer (sdk-php-release.yml pushes sdk/php to keel-sdk-php and tags it vX.Y.Z there)

One-time setup: npm trusted publisher for @keel-context/sdk (workflow sdk-typescript-release.yml); a deploy key with write access on keel-sdk-php whose private key is the secret KEEL_SDK_PHP_DEPLOY_KEY here; Packagist registers keel-sdk-php once (Submit, with the repo URL) and follows its tags.

docs.title: Your first cartridge in 20 minutes
docs.text:
A cartridge teaches Keel your vertical. It is a folder with two files. The core never changes.

cartridges/clinics/
  cartridge.yaml
  handlers.py

Build yours in cartridges/clinics, the folder for your own cartridges. The finished version is in the repo as examples/clinics, with its events in examples/clinics/events.jsonl: point any command below at examples/clinics to run it without writing a line.

docs.title: 1. Scaffold it (1 min)
docs.text: uv run keel init cartridges/clinics

docs.title: 2. Declare the ontology (5 min)
docs.text:
List the kinds of things your product is about and how they relate. Use your product's own names.

entities:
  patient:     { description: A person treated at the clinic., ref: patients.id }
  appointment: { description: A scheduled visit., ref: appointments.id }
  treatment:   { description: A procedure performed., ref: treatments.id }

relations:
  booked_by:   { from: appointment, to: patient }
  performed_in:{ from: treatment,   to: appointment }

ref is a pointer to your table. Keel stores pointers and meaning, never copies of your rows.

docs.title: 3. Catalog the events (5 min)
docs.text:
Write down the 10 to 20 things that happen in your product. Each has a subject kind, an owner team, and a payload shape. This list is the least technical part and the one that saves the most arguments later.

events:
  appointment.booked:
    subject: patient
    owner: scheduling
    payload: { id: string, starts_at: datetime, treatment: string }
  appointment.no_show:
    subject: appointment
    owner: scheduling
    payload: {}

The shipped cartridge adds a third one, treatment.performed, so the treatment kind gets used. Payload hints can be richer than scalars: status: [booked, done] is an enum, tags: string[] an array, items: [ { code: string, qty: int } ] an array of objects, { ... } a nested object (see the specification).

docs.title: 4. Write one handler per event (5 min)
docs.text:
A handler maps a payload to five primitives: upsert_entity, link, unlink, open_fact, close_fact. Ten lines each. close_fact ends the tenant's fact on a predicate; what agents remembered about it (task and agent memory) keeps its own lifetime.

from keel.handlers import HandlerRegistry
registry = HandlerRegistry()

@registry.on("appointment.booked")
def booked(event, store):
    p = event.payload
    appt = f"appointment:{p['id']}"
    store.upsert_entity(event.tenant, "patient", event.subject_id)
    store.upsert_entity(event.tenant, "appointment", p["id"], starts_at=p["starts_at"])
    store.link(event.tenant, appt, "booked_by", event.subject, event.occurred_at)
    store.open_fact(event.tenant, appt, "status", "booked", valid_from=event.occurred_at, evidence=event.id)

@registry.on("appointment.no_show")
def no_show(event, store):
    store.open_fact(event.tenant, event.subject, "status", "no_show", valid_from=event.occurred_at, evidence=event.id)

open_fact closes the previous value of the same predicate instead of overwriting it, and a late event takes its place in the history rather than closing a newer value backwards. That is what makes the graph bitemporal: you can ask what was true on any date. Events are deduplicated by id, so retrying a batch is safe.

docs.title: 5. Add your semantics (2 min)
docs.text:
Definitions your agents should never invent for themselves:

rules:
  at_risk_patient:
    applies_to: patient
    definition: "A patient is at risk of churn after two no-shows in 90 days."
    no_shows: 2
    days: 90
  appointment_missed:
    applies_to: appointment
    definition: "An appointment is missed when its status is no_show."
    when: { predicate: status, eq: no_show }

The context tool returns the rules that apply to a subject's kind, so every agent reads the same definition. A rule with a when is also evaluated for you: context returns evaluation: {appointment_missed: true} next to the rule, so the agent neither defines nor computes it. at_risk_patient needs a count over 90 days, so it has no when and the agent applies the definition. Conditions compose with all, any and not, follow a relation with via (a patient is at risk if any of their appointments is missed: { via: booked_by, direction: in, any: { predicate: status, eq: no_show } }), compare strings with ci: true, and measure how long a fact has been open with open_for_days or open_for_business_days (or how long it has held one of several values, surviving a change between them, with held_for_days or held_for_business_days). The full grammar is in the specification.

docs.title: 6. Validate and run (2 min)
docs.text:
uv run keel validate cartridges/clinics
uv run keel validate cartridges/clinics --events examples/clinics/events.jsonl
uv run keel ingest cartridges/clinics examples/clinics/events.jsonl
uv run keel context cartridges/clinics examples/clinics/events.jsonl patient:P-1

validate fails if an event has no handler, a handler has no event, a relation uses an undeclared kind, a payload hint does not parse, a rule's when uses an unknown operator or an undeclared relation, or the agents, semantic, consolidate or predicates sections are malformed. With --events it also checks a stream against the catalog: unknown types, wrong subject kinds, missing or mistyped payload fields.

docs.title: 7. Point an agent at it
docs.text:
uv sync --extra mcp
uv run keel serve cartridges/clinics --tenant clinic-centro --events examples/clinics/events.jsonl

Any MCP client now sees context, history, search, annotate, related. Your second agent uses the same five tools; there is no second pipeline.

docs.title: 8. Declare your agents (optional)
docs.text:
When more than one agent shares the graph, say who they are and what each may do. The layer enforces it; the agent never polices itself.

agents:
  reception-bot:
    description: Confirms appointments. Writes task memory only.
    writes: [task, agent]
    reads: { kinds: [patient, appointment], relations: [booked_by] }
  clinic-copilot:
    writes: [task, agent, tenant]   # no reads: sees everything

An agent with no writes: may write [task, agent]; one with kind: human is a person and signs as human:<id>. Once agents: exists, every Tools(...) and every keel serve needs --agent <id>, and an id that is not declared is refused. annotate is signed with the agent id, so keel export shows who wrote what. Agent-scope memory is read only by the agent that wrote it; task-scope memory tied to a task id only by calls that pass that task.

docs.title: 9. Search by meaning (optional)
docs.text:
search(text, mode="semantic") finds subjects by meaning instead of by substring. Say what goes into each subject's searchable document:

semantic:
  kinds: [patient, appointment]
  relations: [booked_by]          # an appointment's document names its patient
  split: {patient: [allergy]}     # optional: each allergy (each element, when the value is a list) is also a document of its own, so one long list does not dilute it

Index outside ingest, from a durable store, and serve with the same index and embedder:

uv run keel ingest cartridges/clinics examples/clinics/events.jsonl --db clinic.db
export KEEL_EMBEDDINGS_API_KEY=...    # any OpenAI-compatible embeddings endpoint (KEEL_EMBEDDINGS_BASE_URL, _MODEL)
uv run keel index cartridges/clinics --tenant clinic-centro --db clinic.db --index "examples.custom_adapters:make_index?path=vectors.db"
uv run keel serve cartridges/clinics --tenant clinic-centro --db clinic.db --index "examples.custom_adapters:make_index?path=vectors.db"

--embedder hash runs it offline for a try. The index here is the SQLite example adapter; chroma:///path is the bundled one, and your own vector database is an adapter you write (Connect, semantic search). Run keel index from cron: it only re-indexes what changed.

docs.title: The test that it worked
docs.text: Did you edit anything under keel/? If yes, some domain leaked into the core. Open an issue; that is exactly the kind of thing we want to fix.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
Keel is built in the open at 10–20 hours a week. The order below is deliberate: the public story ships alongside the code, and the proof of the thesis (a second cartridge, a second agent, no second pipeline) comes before polish.

Continue/stop criterion at 90 days: open source traction. Before that, at 30 days: one issue, PR or question from someone we do not know.

docs.title: Next — 0.1 (code shipped early as 0.1.0 on 2026-10-14; pilots through January 2027)
docs.text:
Goal: durable, replayable, and used by two SaaS products that are not ours.

  • [x] Durable store: SQLite (keel/store/sqlite.py, stdlib, same filters as the reference store, --db in the CLI). Graphiti stays a candidate for graph-native queries once a pilot needs them
  • [x] MySQL / MariaDB store (keel/store/mysql.py, requested 2026-10-14; --db mysql://...), a dialect of the shared SqlStore, same conformance suite in CI
  • [x] Replay from an external log (Ingestor.replay(tenant, events=adapter); keel replay ... --db wipes one tenant and rebuilds it from the stream). Event ids are content hashes when the source has none, so a replay yields the same provenance
  • [x] Expire task/agent memory: keel expire <tenant> --db (reads already hide expired facts)
  • [x] keel serve --transport http --http2: HTTP/2 on Hypercorn (--extra http2), h2 over TLS or cleartext h2c; --certfile/--keyfile serve https on either server (0.17.0)
  • [x] keel.client.Client reuses one keep-alive connection, sends User-Agent: keel-context/<version> (Cloudflare blocked urllib's with 1010) and takes headers= and http_client= (any httpx-shaped client: HTTP/2, proxies, retries) (0.17.0)
  • [x] Processes that open one database at once no longer race on the schema migration (facts_key and added columns; MySQL 1061/1060) (0.16.4)
  • [x] annotate(key=) is one write even across processes: a unique facts_key index on (tenant, subject, idempotency_key); a racing call gets the winner's fact back (DuplicateKey in the store protocol) (0.16.3)
  • [x] The table, Kafka and SQS adapters acknowledge only after the Ingestor commits: with batch=N, a batch that rolled back was skipped by the cursor and lost (0.16.2; from the kagent PoC)
  • [x] Ingest no longer slows down as a tenant grows (from the 14M-event stress test, SQLite, same snapshot: 1.0k to 3.1k events/s; context 79 ms to 1.5 ms): relation lookups and changes are two indexed branches instead of an OR that scanned the tenant; the watermark takes one MAX per index (new index relations_recorded); a bulk batch prefetches only the facts it can still change (new index facts_open); SQLite keeps 256 MB of pages in process; keel ingest and replay commit every 5000 events (0.18.0)
  • [x] The example cartridges live in examples/<name>/, each with its cartridge, its events.jsonl and its test_<name>.py (path-independent, so a copied folder keeps a working test); cartridges/ is left empty for a team's own. Paths changed: cartridges/fleet is examples/fleet, examples/events/fleet.jsonl is examples/fleet/events.jsonl, examples/agent_minimal.py is examples/fleet/agent_minimal.py (0.23.0)
  • [x] From the kagent pilot's 41 CUs (more than half the cost was checking and correcting): context(subjects, only=[...]) returns just those predicates, the evidence a reviewer needs from many subjects; a list of subjects is read in batches (facts, proposals, relations, entities: a constant number of statements, it was two or more per subject); search with a list of texts reads each subject's facts once for every text, so many names checked against one subject's neighbours (search(names, kind=[...], related_to=s)) is one call (0.22.0)
  • [x] keel serve --transport http --ui: a read-only browser at /ui (search, context with as_of, a predicate's history, neighbours as a graph) over the same /v1 API; it asks for the secret and tenant (0.23.0)
  • [x] weaviate://host:port: a bundled Weaviate adapter for semantic search (extra weaviate), one multi-tenant collection with a Weaviate tenant per Keel tenant, filters and BM25 inside Weaviate; the official image includes it (and boto3, for keel consume) (0.24.0)
  • [x] From Toche (a tenant per household, Ley 1581): erase a tenant for good. An event declared forgets: tenant in the catalog (no handler) makes the Ingestor call store.forget(tenant) in its transaction: entities, relations, facts of every scope, annotations and applied ids go, a tombstone stays, later events for it are skipped and annotate refused; the report says what was deleted. keel forget <tenant> --db --yes [--index] for operators; the index drops a forgotten tenant's documents (0.24.0)
  • [x] keel consume --queue <sqs url>: an SQS (or ElasticMQ) consumer, one transaction per message, failures left for the queue's dead-letter queue, erasures printed for the audit log (0.24.0)

  • [x] --all-tenants on keel index, keel consolidate and keel expire (store.tenants()), for a tenant per end-customer (0.24.0)

  • [x] From the kagent pilot's second round (semantic search had become the slow call: 17 to 20 s for per_kind with related_to): kind takes a list (listing, semantic ranking and per_kind over just those kinds); per_kind embeds the query once, not once per kind; the lexical leg's BM25 is built once per tenant and kinds and reads only the query's tokens (cached until the index changes; in ChromaIndex also for at most bm25_ttl seconds, since another process may re-index); related_to filters inside the index (where={"subject": [...]}; Chroma collections built before this need keel index --full), so its fused score is now normalized among the neighbours. On a synthetic tenant of 14,000 subjects in embedded Chroma, per_kind=5, related_to= went from 1.76 s to 0.09 s (0.21.0)

  • [x] From the analysis of the kagent pilot's calls (three of four were searches, most for a visual by its title or page): search(where={name: value}) finds entities by an attribute's or a current fact's exact value, in every mode; with kind, text also matches current facts' values; every ranked result says why it is there (matched, snippet); semantic.split makes a document per element of a list value. In the Python client, HTTP, MCP and the TypeScript, Go and PHP runtimes (0.20.0)
  • [x] The 0.19 parameters in the TypeScript, Go and PHP runtimes: detail, depth, perKind, exclude, asOf on search, batches (contexts, searches; lists in PHP), exclude on context, related with a list of relations and depth (each runtime's end-to-end test exercises them against keel serve)
  • [x] What the kagent pilot of technical instructions asked for, inside the five tools: search(detail="concise") puts each result's facts in it (one call, not one plus a context per result), depth=1 its neighbours, and per_kind=n the best of every kind (with related_to and semantic mode, the context for a task in one call); context and search take a list; related(depth=2|3) with a list of relations; exclude and search(as_of=) hide data for evaluations; semantic.split indexes chosen facts as documents of their own. Every parameter reaches the Python client, HTTP and MCP (a test checks it) (0.19.0)
  • [x] An official image, ghcr.io/angelkurten/keel (amd64, arm64; -slim without Chroma), published on every release: non-root, /data volume, its own health check, refuses to listen without KEEL_SECRET; deploy/docker-compose.yml with MySQL, a Chroma server and the indexer. Every command with --db now reads KEEL_DB (index, expire, consolidate and export required the flag, so a container configured by its environment failed) (0.18.1)
  • [x] keel index for a production deploy (from kagent: 11,192 entities took 21 minutes): embedding batches go out four at a time with retries on 429/5xx; the cursor defaults to the index's own folder for chroma:///path (KEEL_INDEX_CURSOR otherwise) and a run without one says it is rebuilding; one run per tenant at a time, a second skips (two at once corrupted Chroma); documented that chroma:///path does not work across keel serve and keel index processes (0.18.0)
  • [x] No N+1 reads: context(depth=1), search(rule=) and rules that follow a relation read their subjects in batches (facts_of, entities_of, optional on a store). On the 14M-event MySQL graph context(depth=1) issued about 100 statements, 130 ms over Docker; now a fixed handful (0.18.0; from the stress test)
  • [x] A store shared by the HTTP server's threads keeps a transaction and a batch in flight to the thread that opened them: an annotate arriving during an ingest batch wrote into that batch and was lost if it rolled back, and other threads read its uncommitted state. MySQL reads on a connection per thread: 32 clients went from 41 to 254 requests/s on the 14M-event graph. Reads of the state now fetch only open facts (facts_open), and rule sweeps that follow a relation read relations in batches (relations_of): search(rule=unit_grounded) 1.0 s to 0.22 s (0.18.0)
  • [x] Ingestor keeps no in-memory copy of the log unless asked (keep_log=True): the HTTP server, the webhook and follow() grew by every event they ever ingested, and a 14M-event load needed about 32 GB (0.18.0; from the stress test)
  • [x] keel sdk python writes rules as a Python literal: a rule with true or null no longer breaks the import (0.16.1)
  • [x] KEEL_TENANT: the default tenant for every command that takes one, and the bound tenant of serve; a product with no end-customers sets one value and forgets it (0.16.1)
  • [x] replay keeps annotations and consolidations; the events land around them (0.16.0)
  • [x] Configuration in a .env file (--env-file, KEEL_ENV_FILE), and KEEL_DB, KEEL_AGENT, KEEL_INDEX, KEEL_EMBEDDER for the matching flags (0.16.0)
  • [x] keel serve --transport http refuses an open API on a non-loopback host unless --allow-open (0.16.0)
  • [x] Generated Python and PHP client() pass timeout and traceparent; Kafka and SQS connect take every adapter option; the unused graphiti extra is gone (0.16.0)
  • [x] MCP annotate takes any JSON value, and detail="concise" reports symmetric relations as both (0.16.0)
  • [x] A handler's close_fact closes tenant facts only; scope=None closes every scope (0.15.3)
  • [x] Scopes never close each other, and consolidation keeps agent memory private and uses world time (0.15.2; from the kagent PoC)
  • [x] Memory scopes enforced on read (0.15.0): agent memory reaches only its author, task memory only calls that pass its task, global memory every tenant from its own partition (__global__)
  • [x] Consolidation (0.14.0): episodic memory into durable facts, declared in the cartridge; deterministic reducers and a Summarizer adapter; keel consolidate, keel expire --consolidate
  • [x] history filters by predicate and scope; context returns the rule evaluation, not only the rule (rules carry a when; context takes as_of)
  • [x] Cartridge validation against event streams (keel validate --events reports unknown types, wrong subject kinds and bad payloads)
  • [x] Third and fourth cartridges: finance (modeled on Toche) and clinics (the tutorial's result), zero core changes
  • [ ] A cartridge written with a pilot that is not ours (logistics?)
  • [ ] Two pilots outside the design customer, running the core for free

docs.title: SDKs generated from the cartridge
docs.text:
The cartridge is the interface definition. keel sdk <language> <cartridge> writes one typed file for your product's repo, the way protoc does; a small published runtime per language holds the HTTP client and the envelope. Decisions and milestones: the design note.

Language Generator Runtime Status TypeScript keel sdk typescript @keel-context/sdk (npm) shipped; tested end to end from Bun against keel serve --transport http Python keel sdk python keel.client inside keel-context (stdlib only) shipped; tested end to end in pytest Go keel sdk go --package <pkg> github.com/angelkurten/keel/sdk/go shipped; tested end to end with go test PHP keel sdk php --package '<Namespace>' keel-context/sdk (Composer, on Packagist) shipped; tested end to end on PHP 8.3

Every generator reads the same keel schema document and writes the same things: a type per event payload, an emit constructor per cataloged event, subject helpers, the rules and constants, and a client factory. --check on any of them exits 1 when the cartridge moved on, for CI.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
keel sdk python examples/fleet -o app/keel_fleet.py

from app import keel_fleet as kf

keel = kf.client("http://keel.internal:8000", "acme-logistics", secret=os.environ["KEEL_SECRET"])
keel.events([kf.emit.tire_depth_measured("acme-logistics", kf.subjects.tire("T-9001"), datetime.now(timezone.utc), "tires", {"unit_id": "MXK-4821", "position": "P3", "depth_mm": 2.6})])
keel.context(kf.subjects.tire("T-9001"))["evaluation"]["tire_critical"]   # True

Payloads are TypedDicts, so your editor checks the keys; a refusal raises keel.client.KeelError with status and detail. A Python product that already imports keel can skip HTTP and call Tools directly; the generated module is for the ones that want the server boundary.

docs.title: Go
docs.text:
go get github.com/angelkurten/keel/sdk/go
keel sdk go examples/fleet -o internal/keelfleet/keel_fleet.go --package keelfleet

Payloads are structs with JSON tags, enums are typed string constants, nullable fields are pointers, and Emit<Event>(tenant, subject, occurredAt, source, payload) returns a keel.Envelope. Errors are *keel.Error with Status and Detail. The output is gofmt and go vet clean.

docs.title: PHP
docs.text:
composer require keel-context/sdk
keel sdk php examples/fleet -o src/Keel/Fleet.php --package 'App\Keel\Fleet'

Payloads are readonly value objects with toArray(), enums become PHP 8.1 enums, Emit::<event>(...) returns the envelope as an array and Keel::client(...) the client. Errors are Keel\Sdk\KeelError.

docs.title: TypeScript
docs.text:
uv run keel sdk typescript examples/fleet -o src/keel-fleet.ts     # in your product's repo
npm install @keel-context/sdk                                         # or bun add

The generated file has a type per event payload, an emit constructor per cataloged event (typed by subject kind and payload), subjects.<kind>(id) helpers, the rules, relations, agents and scopes as constants, and client(options) bound to one tenant and agent.

import { client, emit, subjects } from "./keel-fleet";

const keel = client({ baseUrl: "http://keel.internal:8000", tenant: "acme-logistics", secret: process.env.KEEL_SECRET, agent: "tires-bot" });

await keel.events([
  emit.tireDepthMeasured({ tenant: "acme-logistics", subject: subjects.tire("T-9001"), occurredAt: new Date(), source: "tires.measurements", payload: { unit_id: "MXK-4821", position: "P3", depth_mm: 2.6 } }),
]);

const ctx = await keel.context(subjects.tire("T-9001"));
ctx.evaluation.tire_critical;                                          // true
const depths = await keel.history(subjects.tire("T-9001"), { predicate: "depth_mm" });
await keel.annotate({ subject: subjects.tire("T-9001"), predicate: "assessment", value: "replace", scope: "task" });

A refusal from the server (scope policy, agent registry) is a KeelError with the status and the reason. Keep the generated file fresh with keel sdk typescript <cartridge> -o <file> --check in CI: it exits 1 when the cartridge moved on.

docs.title: The context for a task, in every runtime
docs.text:
The parameters of 0.19 (§7.1, §7.3, §7.5 of the spec) are in all four runtimes. The same calls in each:

Python TypeScript Go PHP Facts on each result search(text, detail="concise") search(text, { detail: "concise" }) SearchWith(ctx, SearchOptions{Text: t, Detail: "concise"}) search($t, ['detail' => 'concise']) Best of each kind, in scope search(t, mode="semantic", related_to=s, per_kind=3, depth=1) search(t, { mode: "semantic", relatedTo: s, perKind: 3, depth: 1 }) SearchOptions{..., RelatedTo: s, PerKind: 3, Depth: 1} ['related_to' => $s, 'per_kind' => 3, 'depth' => 1] Many subjects, one call context([a, b]) contexts([a, b]), contextsConcise Contexts(ctx, []string{a, b}, o) context([$a, $b]) Many texts, one call search([t1, t2]) searches([t1, t2]) Searches(ctx, []string{t1, t2}, o) search([$t1, $t2]) Several kinds at once search(t, kind=[k1, k2]) search(t, { kind: [k1, k2] }) SearchOptions{Text: t, Kinds: []string{k1, k2}} ['kind' => [$k1, $k2]] By a fact's value (0.20) search(kind=k, where={"title": t}) search("", { kind: k, where: { title: t } }) SearchOptions{Kind: k, Where: map[string]any{"title": t}} ['kind' => $k, 'where' => ['title' => $t]] Two hops through some relations related(s, ["r1", "r2"], depth=2) related(s, ["r1", "r2"], undefined, 2) RelatedWith(ctx, s, RelatedOptions{Relations: ..., Depth: 2}) related($s, ['r1', 'r2'], null, 2) Just some predicates (0.22) context([a, b], only=[...]) contexts([a, b], undefined, 0, { only: [...] }) ContextOptions{Only: ...} context([$a, $b], only: [...]) Hide predicates, past instant exclude=[...], as_of= exclude, asOf Exclude, AsOf 'exclude', 'as_of'

docs.title: Runtime options
docs.text:
Every runtime takes the same connection options besides the base URL, tenant, secret and agent: a traceparent sent as the W3C header on every call (Keel stores it with every write) and a request timeout.

Runtime Traceparent Timeout Python keel.client.Client traceparent= timeout= seconds (30) TypeScript client({...}) traceparent none built in; pass your own fetch (one that sets an AbortSignal, or any wrapper) Go keel.Options Traceparent HTTPClient (default &http.Client{Timeout: 30 * time.Second}), plus the context.Context of each call PHP Keel\Sdk\Client traceparent: timeout: seconds (30)

The generated Python client() and PHP Keel::client() take timeout and traceparent too (m.client(url, tenant, secret=..., timeout=10, traceparent=tp), Keel::client($url, $tenant, $secret, $agent, 10, $tp)). The runtime client works the same, and the generated emit and subjects work with it unchanged:

from keel.client import Client

keel = Client("http://keel.internal:8000", "acme-logistics", secret=os.environ["KEEL_SECRET"], agent="tires-bot", timeout=10, traceparent=traceparent)

$keel = new \Keel\Sdk\Client('http://keel.internal:8000', 'acme-logistics', getenv('KEEL_SECRET'), 'tires-bot', timeout: 10, traceparent: $traceparent);

The Python client keeps one keep-alive connection per thread and reuses it, so only the first call pays the TCP and TLS handshake; close() drops it. It identifies itself as User-Agent: keel-context/<version>, since some proxies (Cloudflare's browser integrity check, error 1010) block urllib's default. headers={...} adds headers to every request or overrides the defaults, User-Agent included; the generated client() takes it too.

For HTTP/2, a proxy, retries or mTLS, pass your own client: anything with httpx's post(url, content=, headers=) carries the requests, with its own timeout and pool. Keel stays stdlib-only; the dependency is yours.

import httpx  # pip install "httpx[http2]"

keel = Client("https://keel.example.com", "acme-logistics", secret=os.environ["KEEL_SECRET"], http_client=httpx.Client(http2=True, timeout=10))

keel serve --transport http --http2 speaks HTTP/2 end to end (h2 over TLS, or h2c; see connect); it pays off mostly for many concurrent calls from one process.

Reads follow the memory scopes: agent-scope memory comes back only to the agent that wrote it, so set agent to read your own, and task memory tied to a task id only to calls that pass that task (details).

docs.title: Server side
docs.text: The SDK talks to keel serve --transport http (see connect): one process for many tenants, X-Keel-Tenant and X-Keel-Agent per request behind a shared secret. The server derives event ids (a content hash) when the product sends none, so retries are safe to reason about.

docs.title: Design note: agent registry
docs.text: Status: implemented on 2026-10-14 as proposed, with both open questions decided the same day: read filtering is in v1, and an unknown or missing agent id is refused whenever the cartridge declares agents. The normative text is now SPEC §6.1; this note stays as the reasoning.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: A Tools instance is bound to a cartridge and a tenant, and to nothing else. annotate takes a free-text by; any caller may write to any scope as long as it brings evidence; context, related, search and history return everything the tenant has. That is fine for one team's agents on one box. It is not fine when several agents from different owners share a tenant's graph, when one agent must never write tenant-scope memory, when an agent should only see part of the ontology (a billing agent has no business reading inspections), or when the audit trail must say which agent wrote what and be believed.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
1. Identity. Every tool call is made by a known agent id. annotate records it: by defaults to the agent id, source is annotate:<agent>.
  2. Write policy per agent. Which scopes it may write. Default task and agent; tenant only when declared; global never from an agent.
  3. Read policy per agent. Which entity kinds and relations it may see. Everything else is filtered out of the four read tools.
  4. Enforced in Tools, never trusted to the agent (design rule 5). No sixth tool (rule 7).

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• Authentication. The host (your SaaS, the process that launches keel serve) decides who is calling; Keel takes the agent id as given. keel serve --agent tires-bot binds one server to one agent, the way --tenant binds it to one tenant.
  • Per-user permissions. Keel's unit is the agent, not the human behind it.

docs.title: Proposal
docs.text:
Declare agents in the cartridge, next to the ontology they use:

agents:
  tires-bot:
    description: Reads tire depth, writes task memory for the inspection audit.
    writes: [task, agent]
    reads: { kinds: [unit, tire, inspection], relations: [mounted_on, has_inspection] }
  fleet-copilot:
    description: Answers the customer's questions across the whole graph. Writes tenant memory with evidence.
    writes: [task, agent, tenant]

Absent reads means everything in the cartridge. Absent agents: means no registry: today's behaviour, any caller, any scope with evidence. Backwards compatible.

Core changes, about eighty lines:

  • Cartridge.agents: dict[str, AgentSpec]; validate() checks that kinds, relations and scopes exist.
  • Tools(cartridge, store, tenant, agent=None). With an agent: annotate raises PermissionError outside writes and defaults by to the agent id; the read tools filter by reads.
  • keel serve --agent <id>; the MCP server name becomes keel:<cartridge>:<tenant>:<agent>.
  • keel export already carries corrected_by and source, so the audit trail gains trustworthy authorship with no change.

MemoryPolicy stays as it is (evidence, TTL): the registry says who may, the policy says how. Order of checks: registry first, then policy.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• A separate agents.yaml outside the cartridge keeps a vendor's agents apart from the domain, but then two files must agree on kinds and relations. The cartridge already versions the ontology, so the registry belongs with it. A customer disabling an agent for its own tenant can come later as a tenant-scope fact, not a file.
  • Enforcing in the MCP layer only leaves the plain-function path open. Rule 5 says the layer enforces, so it is Tools.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
1. Read filtering in v1, or writes only? Writes and identity are about thirty lines and cover the audit need. Read filtering touches every tool and search. Recommendation: writes and identity first; reads when a pilot has two agents that must see different slices.
  2. Unknown agent id: refuse with PermissionError, or allow with the default policy? Recommendation: refuse when a registry exists, allow when it does not.

docs.title: Design note: what agentic workflows demand from Keel
docs.text: Status: researched and exercised on 2026-10-14; items 1 to 6 and 11 shipped in 0.9.0 and 7 to 10 in 0.10.0, both on 2026-10-15 (the flow in examples/fleet/workflow_ops.py uses them); 12 stays a documented convention. Two inputs: a survey of the 2025-2026 state of the art (frameworks, memory systems, context engineering, protocols, observability, approvals) and examples/fleet/workflow_ops.py, a deliberately complex flow on Keel (five agents with different registry slices, two in parallel threads, an evaluator-optimizer loop, a human promoting a plan to tenant memory with evidence, an audit) that runs in the test suite on both stores.

docs.title: What the flow showed
docs.text: What happened What it means Triage had to enumerate units with search("unit:") and filter by kind There is no way to list subjects by kind or by rule state; every orchestrator-workers pattern needs a work list Two specialists wrote recommendation on the same unit; history kept both with their author, the open fact is the last writer's Concurrent annotations have no declared policy: last-writer-wins by accident, contradictions are not surfaced The dispatcher approving through the planner's console was refused (planner-bot may not write scope 'tenant') People are principals too; the registry must declare them, and the audit must show who approved context(as_of=30 days ago) answered what was true then, not what the triage saw at the time Transaction time (recorded_at) is stored but not exposed; post-mortems and eval replays need "as known at" A second run the same day would read the first run's task memory Task scope has no task id and no lifecycle beyond TTL Rerunning a step after a failure would annotate twice Durable-execution frameworks replay steps; writes need idempotency keys Parallel threads on one SqliteStore, the human promotion with evidence, the registry refusal, depth=1, the export: all worked as designed The core model holds; the gaps are in enumeration, identity of runs, time axes and write policies

docs.title: What the state of the art says (sources in the research summary at the end)
docs.text:
• Workflows persist state per step and resume from it. LangGraph checkpoints per super-step with time travel; Microsoft Agent Framework checkpoints at the end of each superstep including pending human requests; Temporal, DBOS and Restate journal every LLM and tool call and never re-run a completed step; LangGraph warns that side effects before an interrupt must be idempotent. ADK changes state only by appending events with an invocation_id.
  • Memory systems are bitemporal and scoped, and they never delete. Graphiti keeps four timestamps per fact and invalidates contradicted edges with provenance to the episode; Mem0 scopes by user_id, agent_id, app_id, run_id and marks conflicting relations invalid; Letta documents which shared-memory operations are safe under concurrency (append safe, replace is compare-and-swap, rewrite is last-writer-wins and an anti-pattern).
  • Context is a budget. Anthropic's guidance: return names over ids, offer concise and detailed formats (concise is about a third of the tokens), cap tool results (Claude Code: 25k tokens), avoid list-everything tools but give filtered search; sub-agents return distilled summaries and pass references, not payloads; deterministic serialization keeps prompt caches warm (Manus, MCP 2026-07-28).
  • Protocols moved to explicit handles, subscriptions and tasks. MCP 2026-07-28 removed sessions in favour of server-minted handles passed as tool arguments, added subscriptions/listen for change notifications and ttlMs/cacheScope on results, and carries traceparent in _meta; A2A groups work by contextId/taskId with terminal states; agent identity products (Entra, Okta) give each agent a credential, a human sponsor and per-agent audit logs.
  • Observability joins traces to data. OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions name execute_tool spans with gen_ai.tool.call.id; XTDB's decision-audit pattern pins both valid time and system time to the decision timestamp; the EU AI Act Art. 12 requires automatic event logging over the system's lifetime for high-risk systems.
  • Approval is a durable pause with an id. OpenAI's RunState interruptions, Microsoft request_info ids in checkpoints, A2A INPUT_REQUIRED, MCP multi-round-trip requests; findings are promoted only after verification (Anthropic's long-running harness).

docs.title: Proposals, ranked, all inside the five tools
docs.text:
# Capability Pattern that needs it Size 1 Transaction time: context(as_known_at=) and history(as_known_at=) answer "what did the agent see"; needs the close's own recorded_at on each fact post-mortems, eval replay, Art. 12 S 2 Changes since a cursor: history(since=, subject=None) returns the tenant's facts recorded after a watermark, annotations included; context carries the current watermark incremental runs, background memory formation, blackboard polling, MCP subscriptions S 3 Task ids on task memory: annotate(task=), history(task=), keel expire --task closes a task handoffs, sub-agents on one job, trace grouping (run_id, contextId, invocation_id) M 4 Idempotency key on annotate: same key, same subject and predicate returns the existing fact durable-execution replay, interrupt re-runs S 5 Enumerate: search(kind=, rule=, limit=) lists subjects of a kind, or those where a rule fires now, with a cursor routing, orchestrator-workers, blackboards M 6 People as principals: kind: human in the registry, approvals signed by a declared person human-in-the-loop with audit S 7 Detail levels and budgets: context(detail=concise) returns {predicate: value} and neighbour summaries; limit on history and search; truncation notices name the narrower filter context rot, sub-agent summaries M 8 Conflict policy per predicate: predicates: { recommendation: { multi: true } } keeps one open fact per author instead of last-writer-wins; context lists contradictions across authors concurrent agents on one subject M 9 Proposed vs accepted: an annotation can carry status: proposed; promotion is an annotate with evidence by an authorized principal; context shows proposals apart from accepted facts evaluator-optimizer, approvals M 10 Trace propagation: accept traceparent and tool_call_id on HTTP and MCP calls, store them with each write (and with refusals) so a Langfuse or LangSmith trace joins the audit export observability, "what did the agent see" together with 1 M 11 Freshness in results: the tenant watermark and ingest lag in every context, in a stable position; deterministic key order everywhere agents deciding whether to re-query, prompt caches S 12 Progress notes: a documented convention, predicate: note at task scope with TTL, for agents that must survive a context reset long-running agents docs

Items 1 to 6 and 11 are one release (0.9.0): three new columns on facts (task, idempotency_key, closed_at) with an additive migration in the SQL stores, and extensions to the five tools that keep every existing call valid. Items 7 to 10 are the one after.

docs.title: Design note: ingesting millions of events
docs.text: Status: researched, measured and implemented on 2026-10-14 (design A, SqlStore.bulk, shipped in 0.8.0). The numbers after implementation are at the end.

docs.title: Where the time goes
docs.text:
Measured in this repo (Keel 0.7.1, fleet cartridge, synthetic streams):

Measure Value Round trip per SQL statement, MySQL 8.4 in Docker on macOS (PyMySQL) 0.64 ms Statements per event after 0.7.1 (remember, upsert, link, read facts, close, insert) about 4 3030 events on MySQL, batch of 500 8.9 s (30.3 s on 0.6.0) 101 000 events on SQLite, batch of 500 4.0 s (25 000 events/s) Handlers against MemoryStore (indexed by subject since daad802) 160 000 events/s Parsing and validating envelopes 157 000 events/s Multi-row INSERT of fact rows into MySQL (executemany, 1000 rows per statement) 60 000 rows/s Batched lookup of 500 (subject, predicate) pairs with a row constructor IN 20 ms

So the library's own work is a few seconds per million events; on MySQL 85 to 90 percent of the wall time is network round trips, one per statement. Extrapolated, one million events today would take about 45 minutes on MySQL and 40 seconds on SQLite. Indexes are not the issue: every query uses one and touches one to ten rows.

docs.title: What the literature says
docs.text:
Ranked by expected gain for this workload (sources in the research below):

  1. Set-based batches: one statement per table per batch instead of four per event removes the round trips. Multi-row INSERT is 10 to 30 times faster than row-by-row on MySQL (Karwin: 1M rows, 527 s row-by-row, 63 s with 100 rows per statement and 100 statements per transaction; FromDual: 881 s to 4.5 s on 100k rows). PyMySQL's executemany only rewrites INSERT ... VALUES into a multi-row statement; UPDATE stays one round trip per row, so closes need a CASE/VALUES ROW form.
  2. Group the batch by key in memory so each (subject, predicate) is read once per batch and later events in the batch resolve against memory. Batched reads use row constructors (WHERE (tenant, subject, predicate) IN (...)), which MySQL turns into range access on the composite index as long as the list stays in the hundreds to low thousands (above range_optimizer_max_mem_size it silently falls back to a scan, warning 3170).
  3. One transaction per batch of 500 to 5000 and inserts in primary-key order (done); each extra secondary index multiplies the cost (DoltHub: 4 indexes, 4.4 times slower).
  4. LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE for replays and imports: a further 1.5 to 3 times over multi-row inserts (100k+ rows/s), at the cost of enabling local_infile on both sides and temp files.
  5. Parallel workers by tenant, 4 to 8, each with its own connection, READ COMMITTED: 2 to 6 times, flattening past four. Partition by tenant, never by subject within a tenant, so no two writers share a unique key (concurrent INSERT IGNORE on the same keys deadlocks or stalls, Bug #106610).
  6. Server knobs (innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit, unique_checks), the C driver, multi-statement packets: 5 to 30 percent each once batching exists, some with correctness or ops risk. Not the library's business.

Event-sourcing projections do the same: Marten fetches 500 events per batch and, for rebuilds, aggregates a stream in memory and writes once; Kafka Connect's JDBC sink batches 3000 rows; EventStoreDB stores the checkpoint in the same transaction as the rows.

docs.title: Recommended design
docs.text:
A. Buffered flush per batch, both SQL stores. Ingestor.ingest(..., batch=N) already groups events; the store gains a bulk path the Ingestor uses when the batch is larger than one:

  1. Collect the batch's keys: subjects, (subject, predicate) pairs, relation triples, event ids.
  2. Three batched reads (row-constructor IN, chunks of 1000): open facts per pair, entities, open relations; plus one SELECT of already-seen event ids.
  3. Run the handlers against an in-memory overlay seeded with that state, in event order. Placement and closing (place_fact) happen in memory, exactly as today, so arrival order and provenance keep the 0.4.1 guarantees.
  4. Write back: multi-row INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE for entities, multi-row INSERT for new relations and new facts, one UPDATE ... CASE seq (or VALUES ROW join on MySQL 8.0.19+) for closed facts and relations, multi-row INSERT into ingested. Commit.

About eight statements per batch of 1000 instead of 4000. Estimated for one million events: handlers and parsing about 12 s, four million rows at 60 000 rows/s about 70 s, round trips negligible; two minutes on MySQL against 45 today, and SQLite under 20 s with executemany. A failed batch rolls back whole, as now. batch=1 keeps the current per-event path for streams.

B. Replay fast path (later, MySQL). A replay starts from an empty subgraph, so no reads at all: build the tenant in memory, spill to TSV, LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE. About one minute per million events; needs local_infile on.

C. Parallel driver (later). keel ingest --workers N sharding tenants across processes. Only when backfills span many tenants.

docs.title: Caveats to carry into the implementation
docs.text:
• Keep IN lists at or under 1000 tuples; check SHOW WARNINGS in tests on MySQL.
  • executemany is per-row for UPDATE on PyMySQL: closes must be one statement with CASE or a VALUES ROW join.
  • Memory per batch is bounded by the batch, not the tenant: the overlay holds only the touched keys.
  • The audit seq order of facts is insertion order within a batch; dump and export are unaffected.
  • innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit is global: document it for operators, never set it from the library.

docs.title: Research sources
docs.text:
• MySQL insert cost model and bulk loading: https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/insert-optimization.html, https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/optimizing-innodb-bulk-data-loading.html
  • Row constructor range optimization and its memory limit: https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/range-optimization.html, https://www.percona.com/blog/why-are-queries-with-many-in-values-more-expensive-after-upgrading-to-mysql-8-x/
  • Table value constructors for set-based updates: https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/values.html
  • Measured bulk-load numbers: https://www.slideshare.net/billkarwin/load-data-fast, https://fromdual.com/node/106, https://www.dolthub.com/docs/sql-reference/benchmarks/import, https://planet.mysql.com/entry/?id=2007881
  • PyMySQL executemany rewrite: https://github.com/PyMySQL/PyMySQL/blob/main/pymysql/cursors.py
  • InnoDB locking of duplicate inserts and auto-increment modes: https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/innodb-locks-set.html, https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/innodb-auto-increment-handling.html, https://bugs.mysql.com/bug.php?id=106610
  • SQLite: https://www.sqlite.org/faq.html#q19, https://avi.im/blag/2021/fast-sqlite-inserts/, https://www.sqlite.org/pragma.html#pragma_synchronous
  • Projection practice: https://martendb.io/events/projections/rebuilding, https://martendb.io/events/optimizing, https://docs.confluent.io/kafka-connectors/jdbc/current/sink-connector/sink_config_options.html, https://developers.eventstore.com/clients/dotnet/5.0/subscriptions/

docs.title: After implementation (0.8.0)
docs.text:
SqlStore.bulk(events) is the overlay described in design A; Ingestor.ingest(batch=N) uses it for every chunk larger than one event, so the CLI (500), the HTTP batch and replay get it without changes; streams (batch=1) keep the per-event path. Prefetch reads the batch's event ids first, so a redelivered batch costs one lookup per thousand events and loads no state.

Measure (same machine, same streams) 0.7.1 0.8.0 3030 events on MySQL 8.9 s 0.5 s 101 000 events on MySQL about 300 s (extrapolated) 8.4 s 101 000 events on SQLite 4.0 s 2.9 s 101 000 events re-sent to MySQL (all duplicates) 2.1 s

About 12 000 events per second on MySQL through Docker: a million events in under a minute and a half, write-bound (four million rows at 60 000 rows per second), with round trips no longer measurable. Designs B (replay through LOAD DATA) and C (workers per tenant) stay on the shelf until someone needs more.

docs.title: Design note: SDKs generated from the cartridge
docs.text: Status: decided on 2026-10-14, in progress. The cartridge is the interface definition, the way a .proto is for gRPC; Keel generates the client code for the languages a product is written in.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
1. Both sides in the first version. Producer (emit events with typed payloads) and consumer (the five tools, typed with the cartridge's kinds, relations, rules and agents).
  2. Payload notation: a subset of JSON Schema. The short hints stay (id: string, amount: number | null) and grow enums, nested objects and arrays. Keel translates them to JSON Schema draft 2020-12. Every existing cartridge remains valid. See SPEC §5.5.
  3. Our own generator, with templates. keel sdk <language> <cartridge> -o <dir>. Templates are plain Python modules (f-strings), no new dependency; a template engine only if they get hairy.
  4. Languages: TypeScript, Python, Go and PHP. TypeScript first, validated against Toche, then the other three from the same intermediate model.
  5. Consumer transport: Keel's own HTTP JSON API, described by OpenAPI, next to MCP over HTTP on the same server. Same five operations, two transports; the names and semantics never change per transport (SPEC §7.6).
  6. Distribution: a published runtime per language, generated code vendored in the product. The runtime holds the HTTP client and the envelope; the generated file holds the cartridge's types, constructors and constants, and lives in the product's repo like protoc output.
  7. Tenant and agent per request from the product, with a shared secret. Authorization: Bearer <secret>, X-Keel-Tenant, X-Keel-Agent. The product authenticates its users; Keel takes the ids as given (same stance as the agent registry).

docs.title: Pipeline
docs.text:
cartridge.yaml  ->  keel schema  ->  intermediate model (JSON)  ->  template  ->  <lang> file

keel schema <cartridge> prints one JSON document: the envelope schema, every event with its subject kind, owner and payload schema, the entity kinds, relations, rules (with their when), agents and memory policy. It is the generator's only input and a public artifact: a third party can write a template for a fifth language without reading Keel's code.

docs.title: What a generated file contains
docs.text:
• A type per event payload and per entity's attributes.
  • emit.<event>(subject, payload, occurred_at) constructors that return a valid envelope (id as content hash, when the product gives none).
  • Subject helpers per kind: subjects.tire("T-9001").
  • Constants: rule names, agent ids, relation names, scopes.
  • A Client bound to tenant and agent: context, history, search, annotate, related, plus events(batch) to ingest.

docs.title: HTTP API
docs.text:
keel serve --transport http --db keel.db --secret-env KEEL_SECRET serves one process for many tenants:

Method and path Body Returns POST /v1/events one envelope or a list ingest report POST /v1/context {subject, as_of?} the context object POST /v1/history {subject, since?, until?, predicate?, scope?} facts POST /v1/search {text} entities and facts POST /v1/annotate {subject, predicate, value, scope?, evidence?, by?} the fact POST /v1/related {subject, relation?} neighbours /mcp MCP streamable HTTP, when the server is started with --tenant the same five tools GET /openapi.json the contract

Errors: 401 wrong secret, 403 a refusal (scope policy, agent registry), 400 bad input, 422 malformed envelope. Every request carries X-Keel-Tenant; X-Keel-Agent is required when the cartridge declares agents. A Tools instance is built per request; nothing is cached across tenants.

docs.title: Milestones
docs.text:
1. Payload notation and keel schema. Shipped.
  2. HTTP transport: the API above, MCP over HTTP for one tenant, headers, OpenAPI. Shipped.
  3. TypeScript template and @keel-context/sdk runtime. Shipped: generated for fleet and finance, exercised from Bun against keel serve --transport http; Toche's own cartridge is the next real test.
  4. Python, Go and PHP templates and runtimes from the same model. Shipped: keel.client (stdlib), sdk/go (module github.com/angelkurten/keel/sdk/go), sdk/php (Composer keel-context/sdk); each exercised end to end against the server.
  5. Publishing: npm (@keel-context/sdk 0.1.0, 2026-10-14), PyPI (inside keel-context), a Go module, Packagist. Registry accounts are Angel's step.

docs.title: Open
docs.text:
• MCP over HTTP for many tenants from one process (a path per tenant and agent, /mcp/<tenant>/<agent>, each with its own session manager). Not needed by Toche, whose own MCP server will proxy the five tools; one process per tenant covers the rest for now.
  • Whether generated files carry a --check mode in CI (regenerate and diff) from the start.
  • Streaming or batching for POST /v1/events beyond a list per request.

docs.title: Semantic search: research and evals
docs.text: Status: 2026-10-15. Research on vector stores, RAG and hybrid retrieval, plus a labeled eval bench (evals/semantic/) run with real embeddings. Items 1 to 7 of the ranked list shipped in 0.12.0 the same day and were measured again on the bench (end of this note); item 8 waits for real queries.

docs.title: The bench
docs.text:
Three sandboxes built through the real store primitives, each with labeled queries in seven families chosen to probe known weak spots of dense retrieval (evals/semantic/sandboxes.py):

Sandbox Shape Queries fleet 40 units, 160 tires, noisy inspection comments with URLs, one policy 14 cards 125 Jira-like cards in Spanish, 4 clients, comments with URLs and commit hashes, a pause rule 12 finance a household's debts and dues, Spanish, creditors and amounts 8

Families: paraphrase (no shared word), exact, id ("CUS-1990"), crosslang (Spanish query, English document or the reverse), relation (answerable only through a related subject), negative (nothing relevant exists), rule (semantic query plus a rule filter).

KEEL_EMBEDDINGS_API_KEY=... KEEL_EMBEDDINGS_BASE_URL=https://api.ofox.ai/v1 uv run python -m evals.semantic.run --models small,large

Embeddings are cached by model and text, so reruns are free. A full run embedded about 25 000 tokens per model (fractions of a cent with text-embedding-3-small). tests/test_evals.py keeps the harness working offline.

docs.title: Results (2026-10-15, OpenAI text-embedding-3-small and -large through OfoxAI)
docs.text:
MRR@10 per family, all sandboxes:

Configuration paraphrase exact id crosslang relation rule all (small) all (large) substring (today's text mode) 0.00 0.80 1.00 0.00 0.00 0.00 0.28 0.28 dense (today's semantic mode, cartridge policy) 0.78 1.00 0.45 1.00 0.50 1.00 0.82 0.85 bm25 over the same documents 0.45 1.00 0.80 0.00 1.00 0.67 0.58 0.58 hybrid RRF(k=60) 0.59 1.00 0.88 0.80 0.67 1.00 0.79 0.81 dense + exact-key shortcut 0.78 1.00 1.00 1.00 0.50 1.00 0.89 0.95 convex (0.7 dense + 0.3 bm25, min-max normalized) 0.85 1.00 0.78 1.00 0.67 1.00 0.89 0.92 convex + exact-key shortcut 0.85 1.00 1.00 1.00 0.67 1.00 0.93 0.98

Family columns are the small model. Hit@1 over all positive queries: dense 0.72 (small) and 0.83 (large); convex + key 0.86 and 0.97. Precision@10 on relation queries (many relevant subjects): dense 0.50, convex + key 0.88 (small); 0.75 and 0.88 (large). The offline test caught one impossible label in the first run (a tire that did not exist); these numbers are after the fix.

docs.title: What the numbers say
docs.text:
1. Dense alone loses on identifiers (MRR 0.45 small, 0.28 large): a pooled vector blurs "CUS-1990" into "some card". Today's substring mode gets every id right. An exact-key shortcut fixes ids with no cost elsewhere.
  2. RRF hurts paraphrases (0.78 to 0.59): with equal weight, a weak lexical leg drags good dense results down. A convex combination weighted toward dense keeps paraphrases and still gains on ids and relations, in line with Bruch et al. (ACM TOIS), who found convex fusion beats RRF and is easy to tune with a few labels.
  3. Lexical carries relation queries (BM25 precision@10 1.00): the client's name in the rendered relation line is an exact word match. Dense spreads over similar-sounding cards.
  4. The cartridge policy is not free. Excluding noisy comments did not measurably help these embedders (noise-only equals no policy). Relation lines help relation queries (precision@10 0.50 vs 0.30) but, combined with the exclusion, cost two paraphrase queries: every tire's document now repeats its unit's model and plate, which makes tire documents look alike. Hypothesis to test next: render relations as key plus one label attribute, not every attribute.
  5. A fixed cosine threshold cannot say "nothing here". Positives' top score starts at 0.36 to 0.39 while negatives reach 0.44 to 0.45; at 0.45 the large model drops 21% of positives to silence all negatives. The literature agrees: absolute cosine is model-specific (text-embedding-3 averages about 0.43 where ada-002 averaged 0.85), so any threshold must be calibrated per model, and better signals are a reranker score or agreement between the lexical and dense legs.
  6. The large model buys little once fusion is in (0.93 to 0.98 MRR at 6.5 times the price). Small with fusion beats large without it.

Caveats: 34 positive queries and 9 negatives, written by us, so results are directional; differences of one or two queries per family are noise. Synthetic queries are known to be easier than real ones (higher lexical overlap); real agent queries from kagent and Toche should join the bench.

docs.title: What the research adds (sources in the research summary)
docs.text:
• Hybrid search is standard in production stores: Weaviate relativeScoreFusion, Elasticsearch RRF retriever, Qdrant sparse vectors, turbopuffer BM25. Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval: adding BM25 to contextual embeddings cut top-20 failures from 3.7% to 2.9%, a reranker on top to 1.9%.
  • Seen in our own tests: with 121 vectors, Chroma's HNSW returned at most 90 results however large k was, and which 90 varied when many documents were identical. Keel's widening post-filter loop stops when the index returns fewer than asked, so with an approximate index a filtered match can still be missed. Filtering inside the index (item 6 below) is the real fix.
  • Filtering belongs in the store when a kind is a small slice of a tenant: pgvector 0.8 iterative scans, Qdrant filterable HNSW (99.8% recall at 1% selectivity) and is_tenant payload indexes, sqlite-vec metadata columns. Keel's widening post-filter loop is correct but costs round trips at scale.
  • Asymmetric embedders (multilingual-e5 "query:" / "passage:", Qwen3 instructions) lose 1 to 5% recall without their prefixes; Keel's Embedder.embed(texts) cannot express the role yet.
  • MySQL 9 Community has the VECTOR type but no distance function or index (HeatWave only): not a backend.
  • GraphRAG-style LLM summaries at index time conflict with deterministic ingest; what transfers is query-time fusion and one-hop expansion from top hits.

docs.title: After implementation (0.12.0)
docs.text:
The bench now also runs search(mode="semantic") as shipped (keel) and with an LLM reranker (gpt-4.1-mini through OfoxAI, keel+rerank). MRR@10, all sandboxes:

Configuration small large hit@1 small relation p@10 small dense (0.11 behaviour, before compact relations and the key shortcut) 0.82 0.85 0.72 0.50 dense in 0.12 (key shortcut and compact relations, lexical weight 0) 0.90 0.97 0.83 0.62 keel 0.12 (keys, convex fusion 0.7/0.3, compact relations) 0.95 0.98 0.90 0.88 keel 0.12 + LLM reranker 1.00 1.00 1.00 1.00

What shipped matches the best prototype (convex+key) exactly. Compact relation lines (the other side's key and one label instead of every attribute) lifted dense relation precision from 0.50 to 0.62 on their own. The reranker cleared the remaining paraphrase misses, at one chat-model call per search (about a second with a small model) and a few cents per thousand searches. min_score stays off by default: on this bench the best floor (0.45, large model) still drops 17% of positives.
